chunks.text: Not the sci-fi kind. Not a god in a box. The practical, AGI-like kind this essay argues for — a system that learns a profession, keeps working for weeks, gets better from reviewed experience, and does not need someone watching it every thirty minutes.

chunks.text: Not a fixed artifact with a fixed outcome. A complex system — one where capabilities emerge from simple parts interacting and the engineered structure can adapt. The way a living organism emerges from cells, not from a single blueprint.

chunks.text: The first essay established the idea: large language models, or LLMs, are electricity. Agents are toasters. The structure turns raw power into repeatable work.

chunks.text: This essay extends that idea to a harder question: what would actual AGI look like, and why does scaling the electricity feel like the wrong path?

chunks.text: Scaling the electricity will not build the toaster. It will build a brighter arc.

chunks.text: But here is the thing: do not build a toaster. A toaster is a fixed appliance. Fixed wires, fixed outcome. No matter how much toast it makes, it never becomes a television. It cannot grow new capabilities from experience.

chunks.text: That is the nature of a fixed appliance — it does exactly what it was designed to do, nothing more. If something like AGI emerges from a token generator, it will not be because someone engineered a better appliance. It will be because someone grew a complex system — one that rewires itself through use.

chunks.text: A competent professional is a pipeline: intake, scoping, research, synthesis, drafting, review, iteration, risk management. Most of these steps are not mysterious. They are repeatable.

chunks.text: The hard part is not generating text. The hard part is staying on every step, holding scope, remembering constraints, and avoiding the same mistakes twice. None of that survives when earlier tokens leave the active context window through compaction, pruning, or a new session. We solved the generation problem.

chunks.text: Imagine nature working only with RNA — a family of molecules that includes information carriers and catalytic ribozymes. Now imagine evolution trying to scale that one family into a giant monolith that stores all instructions, catalyzes all reactions, and regulates itself internally. In principle, maybe it could work.

chunks.text: But evolution favored composition over scale. The path to greater reliability was not a bigger molecule — it was more specialized parts working together. DNA became long-term storage. Proteins became functional workhorses. Lipid membranes created boundaries.

chunks.text: Now think about another complex system: the brain. In A Thousand Brains, Jeff Hawkins and colleagues describe cortical columns as association engines: they learn relationships among what is sensed, how the body moves, and what the brain expects to sense next.

chunks.text: LLMs work through a different mechanism, but they reveal the same architectural power in linguistic and semantic space — learning associations across context and anticipating what belongs next. The comparison is not biological equivalence.

chunks.text: It is the shared pattern: intelligence deepens when learned relationships meet, specialize, and coordinate. A single column can learn and predict. A single model can generate and generalize. But intelligence did not emerge from one enormous super-column.

chunks.text: What does differentiation buy you? Each part adapts locally without breaking the whole. Parts specialize without tangling into one giant parameter space. You can swap a module and keep the organism. Fast reflexes and slow remodeling happen on different timescales. And when one part fails, the identity survives.

chunks.text: Here is the smallest architectural feature that changes everything:
chunks.tts_text: Here is the smallest architectural feature that changes everything:

chunks.text: Define a persistent list of jobs on disk (not in the model) — a local file in a structured format like JSON. Mark jobs active or completed — or add whatever states and fields the work demands.

chunks.text: Where the runtime supports it, install a hook that intercepts "Stop" while a job is active, with bounded retries, cancellation, and recovery.

chunks.text: This is different from Ralph Loop's simple prompt repetition. Here, the jobs themselves — their flags, their states — determine whether the agent can stop.

chunks.tts_text: What a year of experience looks like

chunks.text: Imagine two copies of the same model, given the same profession, running for a year.
chunks.tts_text: Imagine two copies of the same model, given the same profession, running for a year.

chunks.text: One has no architecture around it. Every session resets to zero. It improves only when someone retrains it — expensive reinforcement learning runs that touch every weight at once. Between runs, it returns to baseline. Impressive in any given conversation. Amnesiac across all of them.

chunks.text: The practical roadmap
chunks.tts_text: The practical roadmap

chunks.text: If you want to build toward AGI-like autonomy now, do not wait for the next model. Build these four layers:
chunks.tts_text: If you want to build toward AGI-like autonomy now, do not wait for the next model. Build these four layers:

chunks.text: 1) A filesystem brain with compartmentalized memory. Persistent state with clear boundaries — knowledge files, job ledgers, memory stores, and project instructions (AGENTS.md in Codex, CLAUDE.md in Claude Code, QWEN.md in Qwen Code, or the platform's equivalent) scoped to where they are needed.

AGENTS dot em dee in Codex. Claude dot em dee in Claude Code. quen dot em dee in Qwen Code. Or the platform’s equivalent. These instructions are scoped to where they are needed.

chunks.text: 2) A hook system that enforces phases and permissions. Interception points where deterministic rules override probabilistic behavior.
chunks.tts_text: 2) A hook system that enforces phases and permissions. Interception points where deterministic rules override probabilistic behavior.

chunks.text: 3) A job system that keeps the agent alive until obligations are met. Persistent jobs as structured objects on disk. Stop-blocking hooks that prevent premature exit. Observation fields that force the agent to record what it learned before closing.

chunks.text: This is what gives the agent a heartbeat — and what makes self-improvement possible, because the agent cannot skip its own learning.

chunks.text: 4) A consolidation loop that converts traces into durable upgrades. Consolidation phases where logged experience is analyzed, distilled, and written back as improved instructions, refined checklists, and new skills.

chunks.text: Notice that the job system includes maintenance. The agent does not just process work — it also spends compute on itself: managing memory, refining instructions, consolidating experience. Like a cell that does not just process nutrients but also repairs itself, manages waste, and maintains its own membrane.

chunks.text: Why I say "we could have had it by now"
chunks.tts_text: Why I say "we could have had it by now"

chunks.text: Because none of the architecture described in this essay required a research breakthrough. Every primitive — persistence, hooks, jobs, consolidation — is standard software. The only thing missing was the bet.

chunks.text: Earlier attempts at agent autonomy — AutoGPT, BabyAGI, and their descendants — used engineered loops, roles, and task flows. When a fixed plan did not fit reality, it could break. Their limits did not disprove engineering; they showed why state, recovery, verification, and user control matter.

chunks.text: What we needed was complex system design — not defining the agent directly, but defining primitives and letting the agent emerge from their interaction. Hooks arrived in CLI frameworks recently. They are a qualitatively different design.
